Figure 1:OmniShowcaseproduces subject-driven videos that stay
3D-consistent across every revealed viewpoint.

Figure 2:Automated 3D-consistent data synthesis pipeline.From a
curated 3D asset(Deitke et al., 2023), Blender renders the target orbit
and four reference views. (a) The target is composited into a prompt-driven
scene by video inpainting(Jiang et al., 2025); (b) the four views are
reconstructed in 3D(Li et al., 2026)and rendered as the surface-normal
turntable used as the condition. Every stage runs without
human intervention.

Figure 3:Qualitative comparison of training data.Uni3C(Cao et al., 2025)is an image-to-video model, so every surface the
camera path uncovers is generated. Ours renders the subject from a 3D asset
and generates only the background.

Figure 4:Overview of OmniShowcase.FromN=4N{=}4reference views, we reconstruct 3D geometry and render a surface-normal turntable. The reference images and normal condition are injected into the reference pathway of a LoRA-tuned image-to-video diffusion transformer. The model uses appearance information from the reference views and 3D structure from the normal condition to generate the target video without per-subject optimization.

Figure 5:Qualitative comparison with baselines.3DB denotes 3DreamBooth.
Given a teapot and a jar of peach gummies, we compare OmniShowcase against four
baselines. Red boxes mark where identity or 3D structure breaks down.

Figure 6:Conditioning ablation.Given a biplane and a bulldozer,
we compare the three conditioning variants against ours. Marked regions
highlight where identity or 3D structure breaks down.

Figure 7:Additional qualitative comparison.Four further subjects
under diverse camera trajectories, with the same method ordering as
Figure. Each block pairs the four reference views and
the prompt, whose+ [tag]suffix names the trajectory
(Appendix), with generated frames from every method.

Figure 8:Trajectory and scene control.One subject driven by several camera configurations, including arc, zoom-in
and truck, with the background also varied by the prompt for each
trajectory.

Figure 9:Trajectory control in a fixed scene.The same subject and
background under different camera configurations, from full orbits to an
arc and a zoom-out, where only the camera trajectory changes between rows.
Inference only.

Figure 10:3D reconstruction from generated video.The subject is
segmented out of each method’s generated orbit and lifted to a coloured point
cloud, the same reconstruction evaluated by GT-CD, shown here
from four viewpoints so the geometric differences are visible directly.
Baselines recover a thin shell of the surfaces their orbit actually sweeps,
while ours closes the volume.

Figure 12:Camera trajectories.Sixteen representative trajectories
out of the8888the vocabulary defines, one per tag family. Each panel draws
the camera frusta sampled along the path, with the arrow giving the direction
of travel and the grey dot marking the subject.

Figure 13:Failure cases.Left two.Prompt adherence and the
commanded rotation both hold, but the surroundings render with flat shading
and little material detail, so the clip reads as slightly synthetic.Right two.Both receive four reference views of a subject caught in
four different poses. The upper one is prompted in the usual static style
and settles into an averaged pose that matches none of the references, while
the lower one is asked to follow the motion in step with the orbit and
tangles in 3D at the transitions between poses.
